text: The normal distribution is a fine model for symmetric measurements, but plenty of real data isn't symmetric. Waiting times pile up near zero with a long tail. Order values have a few huge purchases. And when we start testing hypotheses, we'll use distributions built for that job. This lesson introduces five continuous distributions you'll meet again and again: uniform, exponential, log-normal, Student's t, and chi-square.

A uniform distribution spreads probability evenly across an interval — imagine a call answered at a random moment within a 10-minute window. In scipy, uniform's scale is the interval width, not an end point, so stats.uniform with loc 0 and scale 10 gives a 30 percent chance of waiting 3 minutes or less, with a mean at the midpoint, 5. Uniform is also what random number generators produce first, and later lessons transform it into other shapes.

If events arrive at a steady average rate — the Poisson situation from Lesson 11 — the gap between events is exponential. Tickets arrive at 4 per hour, so the mean gap is 15 minutes. About 13.5 percent of gaps exceed 30 minutes, and the median, about 10.4 minutes, sits well below the mean of 15 — the distribution is right-skewed.

Exponential is also memoryless: given you've already waited 15 minutes, the chance of waiting 30 more is exactly the same as the chance of waiting 30 to begin with — both come out to 0.1353. That's an assumption worth questioning, since real machines wear out and customers don't arrive perfectly randomly.

If the logarithm of a variable is normal, the variable itself is log-normal — always positive and right-skewed, fitting order values, incomes, and file sizes. Simulating 10,000 values, the mean sits well above the median — 39.97 versus 33.66 — and raw skewness of 2.28 drops to nearly zero after taking the log. That's why analysts often log-transform skewed variables before methods that expect symmetry.

A warning: numpy's lognormal takes the mean and standard deviation of the underlying normal, not of the result itself — a common trap. The t distribution looks like a normal curve but with fatter tails, reflecting extra uncertainty when you estimate spread from a small sample. It has a degrees-of-freedom parameter, and as that grows, it converges to the normal.

With 5 degrees of freedom, you need to reach 2.571 standard errors to cover 95 percent. With 30, it's 2.042. With 1000, it's 1.962 — essentially the normal's 1.96. With a small sample you must reach further than 1.96 to cover 95 percent, and you'll use exactly this in the confidence intervals lesson.

Chi-square and F are sums and ratios of squared normal quantities — always non-negative and right-skewed. You don't model raw data with them; you compare a test statistic against them, as in the chi-square and ANOVA lessons ahead. To recap: uniform is flat, exponential models gaps between events, log-normal models multiplicative skewed quantities, t handles small-sample uncertainty, and chi-square and F support hypothesis tests. Always check your parameterization in the docs.
